utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning, all. May I have the appearances first of all, and we were alerted on our way into court by the usher that there are a number of -- that there may be a number of preliminary issues, and whoever is moving those, perhaps we can deal with that before the witness resumes to take the stand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. It's Joanna Korner and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution. I wasn't aware there were a number of preliminary issues. I simply said I wanted to mention timings. I didn't appreciate there were other issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Stanisic Defence, Zecevic. Well, there is just one issue, which I raised yesterday before we adjourned, and we agreed that it should be brought this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic, Dragan Krgovic, Brent Hicks, and Eric Tully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Korner, your issue of timing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I anticipate taking another hour and a bit with this witness. I've still got a number of documents to go through with him although I'm going to try and speed it up if he answers just the questions I ask. There's then another witness organised for -- well, another two, in fact, for this week. I understand from Mr. Zecevic and Mr. Pantelic this witness will go in to tomorrow with cross-examination. We then have another witness, not Ms. Hanson, and it's simply a question of whether Ms. Hanson is likely to start or not tomorrow, because -- because of the arrangements made, it had been arranged that cross-examination would in any event be delayed. So whether it's worth starting her tomorrow I just don't know, but it seems to me that it's unlikely with cross-examination of the next witness after all of this, plus the videolink on Monday. I'm asked to ask Your Honours on behalf of the lawyer who is calling Ms. Hanson if we can take one and a half hours. It's obviously an important piece of evidence. It's about -- she's the expert on Crisis Staff. So the lawyer says an hour and a half in chief would be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand that the remaining witness other than Mrs. Hanson is ST-13; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And ST-13 is called as a 92 ter witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: May I then ask the Defence counsels if they have made up their mind as to how much time they would need for their cross-examination of ST-13. Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not -- I'm not sure, Your Honours, that I can give you that answer. My co-counsel is not present, and he will be leading the cross-examination of that witness, but I will provide you with the information as soon as possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, ST-13 is -- yes. Just a second, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The e-mail, maybe it will help Mr. Zecevic because we turned up an e-mail we got about him. 30 minutes is what -- 60 minutes, I'm sorry, is what Mr. Cvijetic seems to have estimated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So one hour for Zecevic team to -- you said 60?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, sorry. For us. No, I think it's -- I haven't actually discussed it with the lawyer who is calling him either. I don't think it's more than half an hour. Oh, yes. For us it's half an hour. The Stanisic team sent us an e-mail saying they would be one hour with ST-13, and 30 minutes for the Zupljanin team.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Forty-five, would I say, but we shall do our best maybe to -- depending on the line of answering. Forty-five, I would say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. The Chamber is of the opinion that since the Prosecution asked for Mrs. Hanson to be called on Friday for examination-in-chief, and since we have now twisted the arms of the Defence counsels to accommodate that request, I think we should keep it that way. So if we go on for the rest of this day with the current witness and we finish him off early tomorrow morning and then proceed directly to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- ST-13, then we might or might not finish ST-13 tomorrow, and that spills into next week. So this is why we thought that it might be preferable if we could finish ST-13 today. I don't know if that is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No, sorry. Sorry. We will finish the current witness today, and tomorrow, Friday, we'll take whatever is left for this witness, and then we will proceed with Mrs. Hanson.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. If --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mrs. Korner, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The estimate from both sets of -- oh, sorry. Thank you. The estimate from both Defence counsel for the current witness is two hours each to cross-examine. That means that he cannot be completed within today's session. So he will spill into tomorrow definitely, to be followed by ST-13, who if the estimates are right we are talking about a further possibly two and -- an hour and a half, two hours for ST-13. Thirty minute -- yes. So the most we could probably ask Mrs. Hanson for her name and maybe get a couple of things in, and then she'd be adjourned part heard in -- in examination-in-chief, to come back Wednesday or however long the videolink takes. The videolink at the moment -- or maybe Tuesday afternoon, because the videolink is set for Monday and to go into Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: How is this to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I wasn't here on Monday and Tuesday when this was reflected upon, but it is my understanding that we would prefer that Ms. Hanson goes first before the ST-13 so that we hear her in chief, and that will give us some time to prepare for our cross-examination, because as you know, we received some -- some additional documents very -- very lately about Ms. Hanson. So that was my understanding, that she would be in chief on Friday and then we -- we will cross-examine her probably on Wednesday. So it would be preferable for the Defence if we can instead of ST-13 hear Ms. Hanson in chief and then have on Monday and part of Tuesday videolink, then after that we can have ST-13 on Tuesday, perhaps, and then start the cross-examination of Ms. Hanson on Wednesday. That would be our suggestion if -- if --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I -- personally and from our point of view, we're happy to fall in with whatever the Chamber orders, but I think you'd have to make your peace with VWS on this. Witness ST-13 has been here since Wednesday and that would mean that he wouldn't get in to give his evidence until the following Wednesday. And I don't know what commitments he has either, but that would certainly cause, I'm sure, VWS a problem; whereas, Ms. Hanson is here, works here, so she can give evidence any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is definitely not the first case in this first Tribunal where the witness stays for a bit longer period than anticipated, so I don't see a big problem there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, I've just been reminded. It is a problem because of his work. We had to write a letter to his employer in any event asking that he be allowed to come here. So if he doesn't give evidence on Friday that would cause a serious problem to him, as well as to VWS, plus cost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We have discussed the matter, and we think that the most reasonable solution is to hear ST-13 tomorrow, Friday. But I must also say, and the Chamber was unanimous in expressing its -- its concern about these changes, I think we could have foreseen that Mrs. Hanson finally would not be testifying this week had we been looking more deeply into our crystal ball. So we don't think that if we put Mrs. Hanson off until Wednesday next week that in that case no prejudice will be made to the Defence. You may recall that the whole exercise about having her examination-in-chief was designed to compensate the Defence teams for the inconvenience of having her come early. Now since -- if she's no longer coming early, that is to say, if she would only come Wednesday next week, the Defence should have ample time to prepare for its cross-examination. So the order is that we will hear ST-13 tomorrow, and after when we have finished off this witness, the current witness, and then we will proceed with the videolinks Monday and Tuesday, and if we adjourn early Tuesday then so be it, and you will then be ready to start your examination-in-chief of Mrs. Hanson Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I think there's an added problem I'm not going to trouble the Court with it now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's all -- sorry. I think there's an added problem but I need to check on it before I trouble the Court with it. All I was concerned about was whether Mrs. Hanson would be starting tomorrow, and Your Honours have made that clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: To us it wouldn't make any sense nor any difference really because she would be called only to, basically as you say, state her name. And so for reasons of convenience I think it's best that we now set the time that Mrs. Hanson will be called to testify first thing Wednesday morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, may I -- once may I address Your Honour on this when I've taken some -- taken instructions, got further information in the break and leave it to that, because I think there may be an added problem about another witness. I'm sorry, about this, Your Honour. I'm afraid it's happening because, A, trying to estimate times for witnesses and cross-examination; B, because of the orders about not calling witnesses. We've served extra statements. I'm not going to trouble Your Honour unless it's going to be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mrs. Korner, may I be fair and frank and say that it is exactly this kind of shuffling back and forth that causes the uncertainty in the planning of the trial. I think by now you should be able to calculate exactly which witness can come when. The ban that was -- the two months' ban that was imposed on the Defence -- on the Prosecution, sorry, should now be dealt with, and the initial planning problems that this ban may have caused for the Prosecution should be overcome by now, and -- and I would strongly invite you to ensure that the planning holds from now on so that we don't have to come into these constant rearrangements of calling witnesses. There should be by now a fixed plan for the calling of the witnesses for the next coming weeks. Mr. Zecevic wanted the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I understand the ruling of Your Honours. That's what I wanted to say, and I was wondering when we can make the submissions on the procedural matters. That was the only ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes. Let's have them now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will try to be very short. I understand the ruling by Your Honours that the witness like -- the witness that we are having, who is coming viva voce, the Trial Chamber would like to have his previous statements. I'm just wondering what -- will these previous statements be exhibited in this -- in this case or not? That is the question number one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: They will not be admitted into evidence by the Chamber. If any of the parties seek to have them admitted, we'll make a ruling on that. But the reason why the Chamber wanted to see the statements is that it is an element which facilitates the comprehension -- the Chamber's comprehension and understanding of the witness's testimony if we have been able to read the statements in advance. And in particular, when we come into situations such as the situation we had a couple of days ago where the Prosecution and the Defence were eagerly discussing what was in the witness's earlier statement, while we had not seen the statement. So the Chamber felt completely isolated from the discussion and couldn't understand what was going on because we had not been able to read the statement. This is why the Chamber ruled that from now on we would like to be able to read the statements before the witness comes into the courtroom so as to have a better understanding and orientation of the area and the questions which the witness is going to testify about. They will not be admitted by the Chamber without requests from any of the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but with all due respect, Your Honours, I believe in the previous situation we were cross-examining the witness on his credibility on his previous statements, and they were both exhibited. They were not? Okay, sorry. Now I understand -- I understand -- now I understand the concern of the Trial Chamber. And the second thing -- thank you very much for this explanation. The second thing is, I was reflecting yesterday evening again about the P66, the map document. I'm sorry, but just one observation. I believe the ruling of the Trial Chamber sort of departs from the -- from the guidances. In which sense? Your Honours have ruled that only the documents which are on 65 ter list will be admitted as evidence. Now, this document is not exactly a document which appears on the 65 ter list because it has been redrafted by -- by this witness. And I know it's a small thing, but I just want to make sure that we -- that we have understanding of -- of what are the rules in the court, because I mean, we might come into this situation in the future, and I would like this to be clarified if possible. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think the situation yesterday with P66 was a bit -- was a bit shaky, but the principle stands that for this trial all evidence that comes -- that is finally admitted into evidence and given an exhibit number shall have to come through the 65 ter list, and if a party wants to have a document admitted into evidence and given an exhibit number in this trial, then that party shall have to seek first introduction of that document into the 65 ter list. The purpose of this is for the Chamber to control the inclusion of evidence into the trial. Now, for the map, I understand that the raw map exists as a 65 ter number. Prior to the testimony of yesterday, the Prosecution apparently sat down with the witness and made some markings on the map. Well, I mean, the map was pre-marked by the witness, we understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It wasn't. He marked it in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No, madam --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But there were pictures and a line and a red dot on the map. That is not an original --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes, I see what Your Honour means. We -- we produced the maps with the 65 ter -- with the pre-trial brief in which we indicated where various things were like the police station and all the rest of it. When the witness was shown the maps yesterday, as I indicated in the note I sent, he said, "You've got the police station in the wrong place."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It went back to the analyst who prepared them, who prepared a new map to show it in the right place. And then he made some markings on it when he was giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sure. But -- so what you're telling me is that what was included in the 65 ter list was the original map with this witness's indications of the location of several buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. What was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mrs. Korner, please. What we saw yesterday was a map on which electronic markings had been made, and then in addition to those the witness made an additional marking, a further marking, during his testimony. I'm talking about the first version that appeared on our screen, that is to say the map with the electronic markings. Those, I understand, were added -- or were suggested by the witness prior to his appearance in court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: One change was made to the original electronic map as a result of what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. Now, the ruling yesterday was that as a matter of principle, we would prefer to have the raw maps without any markings, be they electronic or otherwise, because this ensures the Chamber that the markings are really made by the witness himself or herself. So as a general rule, when you come with maps, with photographs, or whatever it is, and you wish to have the witness's markings or indications onto that picture, then please bring the raw picture, the raw material, and then add the witness in court -- ask the witness in court to add the markings that you wish to have included into it. That is the general rule.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just ask on that -- I'm sorry, Mr. Zecevic, but just so I get it clear. At the moment all the maps which are attached to the various municipalities where appropriate have photographs of the buildings which are of relevance, we submit, indicating where they are. That's how they went into the pre-trial brief. If I understand Your Honour's ruling rightly, the witness should be shown a completely unmarked map with the photographs obviously by the side but not indicating where they are on the map. Then if he indicates -- if the witness is able to indicate where these buildings are on the particular map, he should do so, and if they correspond with the electronic version that's been pre-prepared, rather than get him to mark another map with exactly the same indications as has already been pre-prepared, would it not be preferable to use -- no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No, it would not, sorry. It would not. I think if you have the map and you have the photos of the buildings next to the map or aligned in the margin of the map, then you ask the witness in court to draw a line from the building to the place on the map where the building is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So that we would have -- obviously if numbers of witnesses are asked to do it, we would have a number of different versions marked by witnesses, that's what Your Honour is suggesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: If it is necessary for the testimony of that witness, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm just seeking clarification. Thank you, Your Honour. It means, can I just say, we will have to withdraw the present maps from the -- they will have to be replaced with maps without indications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On the question of the previous statements and/or interviews of the witnesses, those being called viva voce, I think Mr. Zecevic has withdrawn his objection. What we've done with this witness's previous statements, as I think Ms. Featherstone has informed, is they're in e-court now so that Your Honours can extract them or look at them on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness may take the bench again, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. I remind you that you're still on your oath. Yes, Ms. Korner. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Djekanovic, I just want to return briefly to a couple of things I asked you about yesterday, if I may. You told us that in accordance with the December 1991 instructions you did establish an Assembly of the Serbian People. Is that right? Can you just answer yes or no, because we dealt with this yesterday. I'm just setting the scene.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We formed the Assembly of the Serbian People of the municipality of Kotor Varos, but I don't know whether we had committed ourselves to the decision of December.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Did the Assembly of the Serbian People meet in the municipal building in Kotor Varos? Before June the 11th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not meet in the Municipal Assembly building in Kotor Varos. These meetings were informal and held at other locations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you just mention a couple of locations where they were held, please.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some of the local community premises. Some of the meetings were in Maslovare, some were in Grabovica, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And they were held, were they, in the two municipalities that you've mentioned, they were both ones which were majority Serb -- municipalities, sorry, places.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were local communes within the Kotor Varos municipality with a majority Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And as regards to the Crisis Staff which we started to look at the minutes of from June, that was, however, established earlier, was it not?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff was formed much earlier, even during the conflict in Croatia when we were receiving refugees and giving material aid to them, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And I just want to ask you about the regional Crisis Staff for a moment, which we've touched on. That was headed by Radoslav Brdjanin, wasn't it? He was the president.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot be sure after so much time has passed. I think that he was for a while at least. I don't know if he was that for the entire period.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, it's a matter of public record, but don't worry about that. You -- did you attend those meetings?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some, yes, but not all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you couldn't go, did representatives of your Crisis Staff attend those meetings?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In most cases, yes, somebody did attend, except for the month of June when we had problems with the roads to Banja Luka because of the conflicts in the Kotor Varos municipality and the lack of safety on the roads.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you see at those meetings Stojan Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did see him at some of the meetings, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what about General Talic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that I attended any meetings where General Talic was present. It's possible that there was one when we had problems in Banja Luka with the roads to Serbia. I think that that was one meeting that I did attend when General Talic was also there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If he wasn't there was there a representative of the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't attend all of the meetings. He did attend some, others he didn't, so I could not really say that a police of the -- a representative of the police or of the corps was present at each of the meetings. At some, yes; at some, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally before we look at the next record of -- of a Crisis Staff meeting in Kotor Varos, when you made the request for a special unit or the request for assistance from Banja Luka for the taking of power in Kotor Varos, to whom did you make that request?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no written request. We had been asking for assistance for a while, probably for two or three months when it was evident that the authority was not functioning in Kotor Varos and when it was evident that the inter-ethnic conflicts in the territory of Kotor Varos were inevitable. Yesterday I said that the majority of militarily fit men of Serbian ethnicity from Kotor Varos --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Please. I'm so sorry, Mr. Djekanovic, but I am going to stop you. That's not an answer to my question, and time is of the essence. Whether it was written or oral, to whom was the request made in the Banja Luka CSB?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We addressed everyone: The corps, the military corps, the police station, the Crisis Staff. We sent the request to all addresses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: To whom in the CSB did you address the request, written or oral? Simple, straightforward question. Who, Mr. Djekanovic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We spoke with Zupljanin and with some others. It wasn't always Zupljanin. There were several persons at different posts. But since Zupljanin was the head of the Crisis Staff and he was from our municipality, it's quite normal that we spoke with him the most.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Now, let's please look at another record of one of your meetings, the 21st of June, and that is 65 ter 702.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're doing that I can't remember whether I made the meeting of the 19th of June an exhibit or asked for it to be made an exhibit. The one we were looking at yesterday with the 65 ter number of -- no, I'll have to ask for that to be marked for identification. It wasn't actually on our 65 ter list, yesterday's. 65 ter 10105. But it's just -- that's one of the imaginary numbers, so can I have it marked for identification, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P77 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You see on the screen there the 31st meeting of the Crisis Staff, 21st of June. You were having these Crisis Staff meetings on a very regular basis, were you, at this stage?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In June it was almost on a daily basis, because that's what the situation called for. Sometimes even twice a day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we come to the part at the bottom where Savo -- and that's Savo Tepic, is it?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Savo Tepic was the -- a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But that's him speaking there, is it?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that it is him. There's nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Highlighted the problem of a lack of personnel for special training of the police. What sort of special training did the police want?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The time didn't permit that, nor was there any kind of special training. The word "special" was quite often used, but it was necessary to replenish the police forces. There was a shortage of personnel. The reserve force of the police had to be mobilised. I don't know of any special training being conducted, particularly at that time in the Kotor Varos municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So it had nothing to do with, for example, techniques of interrogation?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That has nothing to do with that in particular, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "It was concluded that Savo should invite Ljuban or Zdravko to the next Crisis Staff meeting." Ljuban was who?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know specifically who was meant here. It was a long time ago. I don't even know which Zdravko it was. There were two Zdravkos at that point in time in the police. There was Zdravko Pejic and Zdravko Samardzija. I knew Ljuban only slightly, but there was more than one Ljuban, so I don't know exactly which one they're thinking of here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, which Ljuban did you know who was in the police?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know any of them. I had heard of Ljuban Ecim, but there were some local Ljubans who were in the police, so that it's -- it's a name that frequently appears. It's a common name in our area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. We'll come back to that in a moment. And he was -- sorry. And he was there, and that's he, Savo, was given the task of briefing Stojan Zupljanin on problems were experiencing and scheduling a meeting, attendance at which had been ensured from the following persons in addition to the Crisis Staff members: Brdjanin, Peulic, Zupljanin, and other competent people who might be able to help the Crisis Staff in addressing these problems. Stojan Z., who was that?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stojan Z. If you're thinking of the task given to Savo, then it's Stojan Zupljanin that's referred to. I don't know about the rest.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And so where we see Brdjanin, Peulic, and Zupljanin there, the second time Zupljanin is mentioned do you know which Zupljanin that was?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because it's this unit, which was under the command of Peulic, and Zupljanin was one of his assistants, even Chief of Staff at that point or battalion commander, it's possible that this is about Slobodan Zupljanin who was in command of one of the lower ranking lesser units.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who frequently attend our meetings too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Did you have a meeting at which these people attended?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the meeting, the way it was planned to be held, was actually not held. I don't know if any meeting was held where all of these people attended. I don't remember Stojan Zupljanin attending any meeting of the Crisis Staff. We did attend some other meetings together, however, when we were talking with the church officials of the Muslim and Catholic faiths. I don't know of Stojan Zupljanin attending any Crisis Staff meetings though.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I'll come on a bit later to meetings you actually had with Zupljanin, but can you turn to the next page or item 3, which is certainly on the next page in the -- in English, and also I think in the B/C/S. Item 3: "A new proclamation on the return of weapons should be drawn up." Had there been an earlier proclamation that weapons had to be returned to the police?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several proclamations -- or, rather, actions to collect weapons and to place them under control in order to avoid gunfire incidents in the area. I don't know which one you're specifically thinking of or whether it was issued by the War Presidency or some other structure. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't worry about that. All I'm -- but there were orders for the surrender or return of weapons as a result of an order issued by the Crisis Staff, the autonomous region Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't act in accordance with nor were any Crisis Staff orders reaching us at the time, especially this type of orders. This is more of an action than an order, and it has nothing to do with any decisions by the autonomous region Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then finally on this document: "A decision on the proclamation of individual enemies of the Serbian people should be prepared ..." Who were the individual enemies of the Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please help me, tell me where to find that item, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's item -- under item 3 after the bit I just read to you about the return of weapons. "A decision on the proclamation of individual enemies of the Serbian people ..." It follows straight on.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it. Well, please believe me, I really cannot answer that question. I don't know. The way you ask me now, I don't know what it referred to or whether such a decision was made. I don't know if anyone had a problem with that or was placed on any list of that nature or whether it -- this had any kind of practical value.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were there, Mr. Djekanovic. You were presiding over this meeting. Whether it was carried out or not, a decision was apparently made. Who was to be named as an individual enemy of the Serbian people? What group?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat that I don't know any individual enemies. I mean, it says here individual enemies. I don't know specifically to whom this referred. I really don't know. And we did not make any such list ever nor are there any traces of such a list having been compiled.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So it wouldn't have included, for example, Anto Mandic, or Mr. Petrusic, or Mr. Sadikovic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, no, it was never so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. That's all that I ask on that document. Can that be made. That is a 65 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was just notified by my assistants, Your Honour, that there might be a problem with the -- with the document which was tendered as a P77, marked for identification. It's on page 17, 10 to 12 of this transcript. I was notified by my assistants that what was used yesterday was 10106 and not 105. The OTP, therefore, used 10106, and now -- now they said they used 105, which is not correct, and that is -- that one has been marked for identification under P77. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's quite right. I'm sorry, it's my fault.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's quite right. It's my fault. It's 1 -- it was 101 -- 10106, not 5 as I said. So it's my fault. Right. However, this one, this document that we've just looked at was on our 65 ter list, and it was number 702. So could that be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P78, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we just briefly please now move to the -- the hearing -- the meeting that was held on the 23rd of June, which is not on our 65 ter list but has been given the fake number 10107. I just want to ask you about one matter on this. It's under item 1. Two matters, actually. This is Lieutenant-Colonel Peulic informing the members of the Crisis Staff about combat activities in and around the area. He said this: "The situation was stable, a breakthrough by which a corridor would be established towards Serbia, and he informed the Crisis Staff of the operations planned for today, Savo Tepic informed the Crisis Staff of the situation and the police." So at this state by the 23rd of June, you and other members of the Crisis Staff were being kept fully informed. Is that what this says about the military and police operations?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. It's a very leading question. Here is the document. There is no mention the action conduct by the military and police. That's a very leading way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just tell us, would you, Mr. Djekanovic, what the Crisis Staff was being informed about then.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That depends on who attended which session of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On this -- on this occasion, were you being kept, as it says, "of the military operations planned for today"?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At the War Presidency sessions there was never any mention of military or police operations which were to be conducted on that day. Unfortunately, we had a situation in which there were rumours going for a couple of days through the town saying there will be an operation this or that day, but that topic was never discussed at War Presidency sessions. Such a decision was never made, and the War Presidency was never notified of such things.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. So what that sentence reads is plain, downright wrong. Is that what you're saying? You were not given any information about the military operations.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received some information -- or, rather, a brief analysis that covered the territory of Republika Srpska. It was not an obligation on the part of Mr. Peulic, but he just wanted to brief us on the situation on the ground. There was no information or notification of any military combat operations during the Crisis Staff sessions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. I want to be very clear about this, Mr. Djekanovic. Are you saying you knew nothing about the operations on Vrbanjci?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vrbanjci?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Vrbanjci. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several operations in Vrbanjci and in the general region of Vrbanjci.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you were told about them, and you were told about them, were you, by Lieutenant-Colonel Peulic or Captain Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who told you about them?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the day of operations, I with know when -- where they would take place, but no -- Peulic or Zupljanin did not tell me that there would be an operation at Vecici, no, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How about Hrvacani?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, may I?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Of course you can, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I hear you say that you were not informed of the operations to come. Were you informed of the operations that had taken place beforehand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not even that. As part of the situation analyses, we would occasionally receive information on certain operations sometimes, but there were no regular reports on military operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you informed about the -- the takeover of Hrvacani?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want you to think about this, please, Mr. Djekanovic, quite carefully. Are you saying you were not told today?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I was told that Vrbanjci had been taken up or occupied Hrvacani? No. Even if you have that in a document, I claim with full responsibility that such a thing was not conveyed to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we're going to reach a stage which I think is going to require some kind of discussion in respect of what's contained in the interview and what the witness is now saying. It's a situation that has arisen in a number trials, but my application is going to be that I could put to him what he said in interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, so can I just interrupt for a minute. There is law on this as well, on this issue. I don't know if there's going to be any argument from the Defence. If there is, maybe the witness ought to withdraw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Witness, do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Then I would kindly ask you to take off your earphones. The --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There was a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- situation, I suppose, is whether you will be asking for the right to cross-examine your own witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly. I mean, that's in essence what it comes down to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But that requires a formal request from your side.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm making the request now, Your Honour. That's the point. I couldn't make the request before the situation arose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Are you now asking the Chamber to declare this witness a hostile witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- which will allow you to cross-examine? Be specific about what it is you want.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I am, but it's an interesting -- the rules don't actually deal with a question of a hostile witness. It's not like a common law situation, and that's always been the interesting part of practice here. There is no specific mention in the rules of either leading or non-leading questions or indeed when a witness is -- should be treated as hostile. We are calling a witness who in essence, as Your Honours can tell, is not sympathetic to the Prosecution's case. In a common law situation that wouldn't happen, because it's clearly a witness is one side or the other. As my understanding of the civil law is, that doesn't apply because the witness is there at the -- effectively at the Court's request. There's, therefore -- and presumably that's because the rules were drafted by a mixture of those who come from a civil law background and a common law background no mention of hostile witnesses, but I'm certainly saying, we've called this witness because we feel that Your Honours need to hear from people who were on the other side and not just from those who are victims, alleged victims of what happened. In so doing, we have a problem in that they are not sympathetic, and particularly where they've said one thing to us in interview and are now saying another thing in court, we are asking for leave, if that's required, to, as you put it, cross-examine our own witness. And as I say, there's a -- there's an Appeals Chamber decision in the Popovic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You indicated that the rules are -- just a moment, Mr. Pantelic -- that the rules are specifically silent on this point, but within the framework could you direct me to the -- such rule exists on which peg you hang the present situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm hanging it on the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, Your Honour. I can't -- there's no peg in the rules. It says one side calls his witnesses and the other side calls his witnesses but the rules are specifically silent on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And the Popovic appeal ruling says what?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The Popovic appeal ruling says -- I've just been handed it -- that a calling party must -- I'm just going to the very last page of the decision Your Honour. "The calling party must seek the permission of the Trial Chamber to impeach its own witness in relation to the credibility of that witness or the substance of his or her testimony and the scope of challenge must be subject to the control of the Trial Chamber." Effectively we can do it but we have to apply to you for permission and then you control how much, how far we can go. I can get copies of the whole decision for Your Honours if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And you say you're now making that formal application.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I am. Because the witness, in our submission as you will see, said something directly contrary to what he said in interview. Indeed he says -- and he actually referred to it obliquely by saying he may have said something else on paper but he's now changing his mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honours. Yes. The essential here about this particular situation is that as my learned friend Ms. Korner mentioned that we are here dealing with the so-called hybrid of two systems: Common law and civil law. So I believe that following this arguments this witness should be questioned along the lines of his personal knowledge on the direct questions of the situations in accordance with the principle of civil law, because he is OTP witness in chief. You are sitting here as a Trial Chamber to conduct these proceedings, and of course you are also allowed and you will exercise your right to pose any questions you might think which are important, like you did in previous -- previous situation. That's a first level. Second level is the specific -- second level -- [Trial Chamber and senior legal officer and registrar confer]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honours. Second issue is that my learned friend Ms. Korner, during the process of interviewing this witness, misused her capacity and on many occasions she put it suggestive and -- and leading questions to this witness where he was at that time questioned in capacity of suspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Are you giving evidence now, Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, no. I'm not giving evidence. I'm just making submissions relating to the circumstances around this witness. And even now he should be warned that answers which might be answered by him might incriminate him in any future proceedings. So that's the point of my submission. I do not agree with the approach taken by OTP in this particular situation, because they should limit themselves only on the line of question regarding this witness and his personal knowledge about certain situations. Otherwise, he is not a witness. He doesn't have capacity to be a witness, because his personal answers might incriminate him, and we don't see any particular warnings towards that. So thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Unless I have missed something you have said, Mr. Pantelic, I don't -- you aren't taking issue with the jurisprudence on this point that where in the OTP's view there is such an inconsistency between the viva voce testimony of the witness and a previous statement that they cannot seek to -- and I'm trying to avoid the language of a hostile witness, but they are not prevented from seeking to do what they are now implying. You aren't saying that. I understand your -- the thrust of your reservation, but you aren't going so far as to suggest that they can't do what they're now seeking to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's exactly the point and the ground of my submission, because, you know, with this twisting of -- of strategy in approach of this -- to this witness is really without any grounds in -- in legal and jurisprudence issues. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But you would have the opportunity, of course, in cross-examination to deal with this, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. I will be in situation, Your Honour, but you know, this is a specific moment that we have to react, because this witness was -- might be confronted with certain answers that he gave in a previous proceedings; namely, the process of interview made by OTP on a line where they didn't fulfil all standards of diligence in this -- in this situation. They -- they submit this witness to -- to leading questions, and they practically created a kind of situation which is not applicable to this particular moment that we have here. So I really object to -- to any reference to previous interviews that this witness gave to the OTP. So he is here. They have questions. They have line of questions. He can answer, yes, no, remember, don't remember, simply as that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, would it assist, it's pretty close to the break anyhow if I were to get copies for you before you rule on this of the decision in Popovic and also I can also provide it to my learned friends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, did you wish to be heard on this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I fully agree with what Mr. Pantelic is saying. I understand his reservations and I share them. I'm not sure I understand all of it, but the part which I understand I do share, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Yes. We will take the break at this point then.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We'll get copies through your legal officer of the decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. We have been alerted that in the extended break when the Chamber's been considering this procedural question that counsel has been similarly industrious, and, Mr. Zecevic, you would wish to further assist us on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I hope that I will assist you. It's just that we did a quick research on the subject, Your Honours, and I would like to raise a couple of issues. I think it will assist the Trial Chamber in taking the decision. First of all, let me just briefly say what I started. I think the facts which are undisputed is that this witness has been -- has been interviewed as a suspect, that's number one; and the second thing, what we have is not his statement, it's just the transcript of his interview in English, and he doesn't speak English, so there was no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, could you repeat the last point you just made.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Witness was interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor and their investigators as a suspect. That is number one. The second thing is, his interview, it is not the statement what he gave. He gave an interview, and it has been transcribed in English language which he doesn't speak. So he didn't have any opportunity to correct possible mistakes. Those are the facts. Now, Your Honours, it come to my attention that the law on the transfer of cases from the ICTY to the prosecutor's office of BiH and the use of evidence collected by ICTY in proceedings before the courts in BiH of 2004, which is applicable right now in -- in the country where the -- where the witness comes from, in Article 5 really does give the opportunity of the state court of BiH to use the evidence of this witness in the proceedings before that court. Now, I have researched the -- the European Court of Human Rights, and I would like to draw attention of Your Honours to a number of cases. Marttini v. Finland, Shannon v. United Kingdom, and Heaney & McGuiness v. Ireland. Basically what these cases are saying, what is the jurisprudence of the European Court of law. Basically comes down to the finding of the court that the appellant's right not to self-incriminate goes beyond the right to refuse individual questions, meaning that he cannot be forced to respond to the questions and then that be used against him, in fact, self-incriminating him. This raise -- this raises a concern with me, Your Honours, which I -- which I wanted to share with you that I think that the witness should be at least assisted by -- by an advice of the counsel in this matter. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I think there's a point for clarification. As far as I understand the matter before us, the issue is not whether this witness can be held responsible for his actions relating to the events in 1992. That is not the issue. He's not -- the issue which we had before us here in this court today is not whether he should be regarded as a suspect in relation to the events during the war. The issue here is only whether the witness is testifying truthfully, and I think the impression that this witness had made -- has made on the Chamber, or at least has made on me, is that because of his -- his knowledge of the events that took place in 1992, he may not have testified with very much precision. I have understood some of his answers to us during the course of his testimony here to be somewhat vague, and I understand his reasons, and I think we should make it clear to him that he will not be prosecuted before this Tribunal because of what he has testified. Now, whether his testimony here may be used before the special court in Sarajevo is another matter, but in any case, he is required to testify truthfully and accurately before us in this courtroom. So when it comes to the issue of his previous interview, I fully appreciate the fact that this interview was made not as an ordinary statement made by the Prosecution's investigators, but was conducted as an interview in which he was himself a suspect and that he was told that he was a suspect. So that, of course, puts the interview in a very special light. But we will take this into consideration if ultimately we allow the Prosecution to confront the witness with what he is saying -- with his interview back then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. I fully agree with your assessment. It is not the -- you're 100 per cent right. It is not the case before this Tribunal that he is suspect or anything. There is no pending investigation as far as we know. But he is a suspect in his country, and his country, by the rule of the law has the power to use his statement over here in order to use it before the court of law in his country. Therefore, what I'm concerned about is the witness -- there is no doubt that the Trial Chamber has the wish to have a truthful answer from the witness, but if this truthful answer would ultimately self-incriminate him, then I would have a problem, Your Honours, and I think we should -- that he should be cautioned and get separate legal advice on how is he to -- supposed to -- to answer these questions before this Trial Chamber. That is my concern, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But just to reply to that, as far as I have understood, but we can ask Mrs. Korner about it, but as far as I have understood the questions that have been put so far to this witness, these questions do not seem to implicate the witness in terms of possible criminal proceedings in Sarajevo. The questions have so far, and I think correctly, been addressed to the witness in order to elicit evidence from this witness about the participation and the role of your client and of Mr. Zupljanin, especially Mr. Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in essence that is true, but, Your Honours, the few last questions, I believe, have been directed directly against in my -- at least in my view and my opinion against this witness, and that is why ultimately our friend from the Prosecutor's side ask that he be treated like a hostile witness. That is my concern. Thank you very much. I'm sorry I took some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. If I may, I fully support the submission of my learned friend Mr. Zecevic, and I would like to outline another very important aspect of this particular issue. Mr. Djekanovic, being treated or qualified as a hostile witness will be in situation that in relation to the law of co-operation between the jurisdiction of BiH and Tribunal might be confronted with certain criminal proceedings there. He needs legal advice. He needs to be informed about all aspects of possible consequences of his testimony here and confrontation with the previous statement that he gave to the OTP, and I think the Association of Defence Counsel here in the Tribunal should be informed immediately about this particular situation, because now we are entering into the sphere of the basic rights of a person to be informed about the consequences, to be informed about the possibility to have legal advice and aid, and so on and so forth. I don't have, Your Honours, any problem if Prosecution will treat him as before like OTP witness on the 65 ter list, but I have, personally as a professional, this is actually the basis of my Code of Professional Conduct, I have a problem seeing the possible violation of an individual's right here without putting my submission on the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic and Mr. Zecevic, what you are suggesting is that the Prosecution cannot cross-examine this witness without somehow implicating him in the events that took place during the war, and this is where, at least from my own personal point of view, I may differ from you, because I think that it would be possible to cross-examine a witness, even it is done by the calling party, for the purpose of eliciting evidence that relates to the accused in this case. I don't see that necessarily confronting this witness with what may have told the Prosecution's investigators earlier on that this would necessarily have to imply any criminal responsibility on the part of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I agree with you if we are speaking of the potential and future proceedings against this witness before this court, but this witness needs now, at this moment, he needs a personal legal advisor sitting beside him if he will be confronted with an interview that he gave to OTP in his capacity of a suspect, simply as that. Otherwise, he can -- he should be informed but not -- well, in part by you but not by us or by OTP, but with an independent legal advisor of the consequences of the possible answer that he will give in confrontation with his previous statement which was made under a specific mental condition where he was a suspect in the office of the prosecution in Sarajevo, and that certain development of his testimony now might -- might have very, very serious consequences for him. That's my point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour, the Defence counsel -- I'm sorry -- are muddling a number of different concepts at the moment. The first is the application that I made which is simply to treat, putting it in its common law session -- way, this witness as a hostile witness, in other words, hostile to the Prosecution's case. That is a separate in itself and there is ample jurisprudence from this Tribunal that, subject to Your Honours' leave I should be allowed to do it. That's perhaps that matter, and they're not really dealing with that matter, because as Your Honour Judge Harhoff has pointed out, putting to him what he said in his original interview doesn't necessarily implicate him in anything. The matter that they're now raising is a matter that effectively, virtually since the trial of Brdjanin, which is the first -- in what I call insider witnesses gave evidence has come up over and over again, and that is why Rule 90(E) is in place. Clearly where witnesses who are called who are suspects within the meaning of the rules in that they are implicated in the events of -- which this trial is dealing with, and indeed this witness is so implicated from the fact of his position and the actions he did or did not carry out, should give evidence to enable the Trial Chamber to arrive at the truth of what happened, and therefore, it's quite clear why Rule 90(E) was passed. The situation of such witnesses giving evidence in these trials has continued since the state court, not only in Bosnia but also in Serbia and Croatia, took over war crimes. The reality is that is why it is said under Rule 90(E) it's the witness's privilege to object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate him. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against the witness for any offence. And, Your Honour, the reality is once that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Please read the sentence to the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Other than false testimony, yes. I'm sorry. I'm leaving aside perjury for the moment. Your Honour, that's one thing obviously one can show that when compelled, he told a complete lie, that's one thing. But the reality is although the case papers concerning this witness, for example, may be sent to the state court, once he's been compelled in this way to answer - and can I say that I spent some months in setting up the war crimes court in Sarajevo, in the Prosecutor's office - it cannot be used against him. It's not admissible against him even in a proceeding in the state court, and that I know is the situation that is being followed. So from that point of view, it's not a valid argument made by Mr. Zecevic or Mr. Pantelic, but as I say, at the moment that's an entirely separate issue. All that Your Honours are considering at the moment is whether or not on this particular aspect, namely, whether they were told about the actions in these various towns he said something totally different in the interview to what he has now said to the Court. That's all I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just very quick, Your Honours. I appreciate what Ms. Joanna Korner said about the law in BiH, but I have provided the copies to Ms. Featherstone and to all parties of that particular law, and let me read Article 5: "Evidence provided to ICTY by witness --"

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just a moment. Can I have a copy? You haven't given us a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I sent it by mail. Well, I'm sorry, I don't have the means to print it out in court. "Transcript of testimony of witness given before the ICTY and records of the positions of witnesses made before the ICTY in accordance with Rule 71 of the ICTY RPE shall be admissible before the courts provided that that testimony or this position is relevant to a fact in issue." Under 2: "The Court may exclude evidence given by a witness with protective measures where the probative value is outweighed by its prejudicial value." And 3: "Nothing in this provision shall prejudice the defendant's right to request the attendance of witnesses referred to in paragraph 1..." and so and so on. It is my reading that this Article 5 gives the power of the Trial Chamber in Sarajevo, in Bosnia, to use this -- the testimony of this witness, and in that respect I do not agree with the overview that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That's notwithstanding our own Rule 92(E)?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry? You mean Rule 90(E)?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Rule 90(E), yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, just one word. Again for the record. This man, Mr. Djekanovic, needs a legal help. He needs to -- I don't know, whether it's the registry who will take care about his rights, but definitely before entering in any kind of scenario here, he needs legal advice. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantelic. We have discussed the matter, and the ruling is the following: That according to the Appeals Chamber's most recent decision of 1st of February, 2008, in Popovic, we can divide the proceedings here into two steps: The first step is that we can allow the Prosecution to confront the witness with an earlier interview or statement without having to declare this witness adverse or hostile, but only for the limited purpose of clarifying one particular issue and only one, and this is what we will do. So we will allow the Prosecution to confront Mr. Djekanovic with his earlier interview but only for the limited purpose of clarifying whether or not he was informed of the actions taken as a part of the military operation and for that purpose only. For this, we do not need to declare him hostile at this moment, and for that same reason we do not see it necessary to have a counsel. Now, if during the further examination of this witness the same problem arises again, then we will proceed to step two, which is then to declare him formally, upon the Prosecution's request, an adverse witness. And I'm using the term "adverse" in order to avoid the special connotation under common law that applies or that attaches to the expression "hostile." So we will call him adverse. But if the problem continues during the further examination-in-chief, then the Prosecution may ask the Chamber to declare him an adverse witness, and then we may proceed to do so with the consequence that from that point on the Prosecution can cross-examine him and put earlier and other statements to him in order to challenge his -- to impeach his credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes. Just for the record, I think that the particular inconsistency we're talking about is not only about the military operations but as well the police operations. Both military and police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just so it's clear, this particular inconsistency relates specifically to the military actions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do the parties agree to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is your ruling. We have to accept it, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's an absolutely reasonable ruling, but if I well understood you, for the other line of questioning that you might allow, I believe, and I again outline my position that he should have legal advice prior to enter to this second line of questioning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, it was your own submission that you would have no objections to the Prosecution continuing to examine him in chief as a viva voce witness, and that is exactly what we'll do, and if, as I said, if the problem occurs again, we will then consider a request from the Prosecution to declare this witness adverse, and at that point we will also consider to supply him with a counsel, and the registrar is currently in the process of checking out with the ADC whether there is a counsel available for this purpose. So we are preparing ourselves for that. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It was my understanding, too, so thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Djekanovic, I'm going to give you one last chance to answer the question before I show you the interview. Did you, as is stated in that document that we were looking at, the 23rd of June, 1992, get a briefing from the military about the operations they were carrying out?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, from time to time, occasionally at some sessions there were some tentative briefings, very superficial, and I do not in any way claim that there were no such desultory bits of information at that session, but as to what type of means would be used and where exactly we had no such information. No mention was made at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. In which case, do you agree you were informed about - and I keep mispronouncing this - Vrbanjci? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically what operation or action are you referring to I'm not sure, but from time to time I was informed on actions in Vrbanjci as well as some others.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the others included, didn't they, Hanifici, Crko Brdo, and Kninska?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cirkino Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were told about those operations, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically. Not separately. I was not informed of those operations, nor was it anyone's duty to inform me thereof.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, then if -- we keep getting side-tracked. If it wasn't their duty to inform you of it, what was the purpose of Lieutenant-Colonel Peulic attending the Crisis Staff meetings then?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the needs of the army -- or, rather, for their normal functioning it was necessary to provide supplies in the rear -- or, rather, logistics. We needed to provide them with clothes, shoes, foodstuffs. There was a lack of all of these items. It was necessary to take out the wounded, to take them for treatment, those who were wounded, to inform their families, and so these were the aspects where we received detailed information so that we could take measures on our part.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to leave the topic. Can you just look, however, at the next page of the document in English. It's the same page, actually, in B/C/S, but it's page 2 in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's the same document we were looking at. You mean you've taken it off. In English it's two pages. In B/C/S, you're right, it's one page. 23rd of June. Okay. It's all one page. I'm sorry. It's just a different copy of the translation. Is the B/C/S up? Yes. Thank you. And the English up, please, as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Under item 2, the members of the Crisis Staff are to -- who are to go to Banja Luka to carry out certain tasks were designated. What were the tasks to be carried out in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was necessary to provide food. We were to find such foodstuffs. Also, fuel. We also had to find donors in order to provide these supplies, because all normal supply routes were cut off. There was no electricity. The phone lines were down. There were no medicines. And we had dead people on a daily basis. They had to be buried. We had to visit their families and provide them with some form of subsistence. And this was the most frequent reason why we went to Banja Luka, because that's where we sought all these means in order to provide a normal existence for these people as much as we could.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. And was that assistance sought from the Crisis Staff of the autonomous region?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we sought assistance from companies, from individuals, donors, and also from the regional Crisis Staffs. Why not? We sought to find assistance wherever we could in order to provide any minimal quantity of fuel, if we could, and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to move to the next meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that just be marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P79, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we then move, please, to 65 ter number 075. The meeting of the 24th of June. Under item 3, please: "Inspector Pejic informed the Crisis Staff about the work of the security service and the results of the questioning of the persons who had been brought in." Now, is that the inspector Pejic that you referred to who had the first name of Zdravko?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the only inspector Zdravko Pejic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was he telling you about the results of the questioning?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, 17 years on I can't really recall the things that he mentioned then.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did he tell you that he had questioned, for example, Mr. Petrusic who was the --

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That was fairly quick. Or Anto Mandic or anybody like that?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not discuss the questioning of these individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, then, can you -- can you think back? I mean, this dramatic period of your life, Mr. Djekanovic. What was he telling you about the questioning?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I cannot really recall the details of the questioning, whom it was that he questioned, and 17 years is really a long time, and I can't recall the details. If there were -- if there was any more detail in these minutes perhaps that would jog my memory, but just off the top of my head I really can't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He goes on to suggest that a session of the Crisis Staff be devoted to the problem of detained persons. What was the problem of detained persons?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a number of ways in which persons were detained. One of the ways, and this was of concern to the Crisis Staff staff and where we engaged in some sort of action, was in the situation where there were families who had been abandoned after certain combat operations and the families were not provided for. And frequently those families themselves would just come and seek for some kind of protection so that they could be put up and accommodated somewhere. And for the most part, most of the time we discussed how to provide accommodations and where for those families, how to feed them, to provide them with food, because I've already mentioned before what the living conditions were then and all the things that we did not have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Djekanovic. Are you telling us that the word "detained" effectively means people who've been made homeless? Is that what you're telling the Court? As opposed to people who had been imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this refers more to people who did have their homes, but these homes were exposed. They were not protected. There were a lot of armed members and armed groups milling around. They were from all sorts of structures. These people did have their homes, but they did not feel safe there, and they sometimes felt they needed to leave them and seek some sort of protection or shelter. Sometimes they wouldn't even -- they weren't even sure that they would reach the next morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... simply inspector Pejic allegedly informed me about the detained persons known Serb nationality who allegedly committed blah, blah, blah and they were in the prison and they were questioned by the authorities. Because here we're going along the lines whether it was some kind of people, displaced people, et cetera. It doesn't have any sense this kind of -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I must say I'm amazed by that interjection. Absolutely amazed. One it's improper, but, two, is it now suggested that I should put to the witness that he's certainly not telling the truth and this is all about people who have been captured and imprisoned? Is that what Mr. Pantelic would like me to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
