utterances.text: No, Ms. Korner. I mean, of course you can do whatever you think that's appropriate to do, but I'm telling you that this transcript is not logical due to your maybe unprecise question or maybe due to the interpretation, because this witness is speaking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- about displaced person and you are thinking about the people who were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- detained. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think this can be sorted out during your cross-examination. I think we should leave it for the moment to Mrs. Korner to complete the examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just try to help Ms. Korner in this respect. I believe there is a slight ambiguity about the -- about the translation of this, because the word in Serbian which is written on this document does not clearly, hundred per cent, correspond to "detain," to be "detained." So maybe that could be clarified with the witness. Maybe that's the reason for miscommunication between Ms. Korner and the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. What does the -- can you just read out, so that I can get a translation, please, the sentence that begins, if it does begin, "He suggested." Can you read it out from the actual original document.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He proposed that a meeting of the Crisis Staff be devoted to the problem of persons who had been detained or brought in. After the discussion of the work of the security station, it was concluded that the Crisis Staff has no right --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It wasn't, was it, Mr. Djekanovic, that Inspector Pejic was talking about people who had been made homeless. He was talking about people who had been arrested and brought into the police station.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember session -- that Pejic talked about interrogating persons who had been detained at the public security station, at the Crisis Staff, and the Crisis Staff was not authorised over such matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's -- all right. Let's move on to the next sentence which you started to read. "After a discussion of the work of the security station, it was concluded that the Crisis Staff had no right to interfere in the professional work of the police and the army and that no one wishes to ... take upon itself security and the creation of conditions..." et cetera. As far as you were concerned, did the Crisis Staff have the authority to order the police what to do and how to do it?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the Crisis Staff did not have that authority. The Crisis Staff only sought the assistance of the police occasionally when it was necessary to secure or to provide protection for certain people or for certain persons or families. We could not issue orders to the police. We didn't have the right to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So who had the right to issue orders to the head of the SJB in Kotor Varos, namely Savo Tepic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never worked at the MUP and am not familiar with the organisation and the hierarchy of the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. We'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that then, please, be exhibited as it's on our 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P80, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 26th of June, please, which is exhibit -- 65 ter 707.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This particular meeting, no doubt, Mr. Djekanovic, you do remember quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is your assumption. I really only slightly recollect these events, and in the preparation for this hearing a few days ago I read something. Some things I saw for the first time, but as for the nature of that, I don't recall -- it is my nature I don't recall things that happened three days ago or something. So I'm not able to remember things that happened 17 years ago in every detail. Of course, I do recall generally what happened, but I don't remember each move, each detail, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, if we look at that, and you had a chance to read it yesterday and you were asked about it in interview, this meeting came after the killings, didn't it, outside the medical centre in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but this was preceded by some other events.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, what was preceded by some other events, the killings or this meeting?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The killings preceded the meetings. There were killings. There were some of our people who died. There were ambushes, killings, and then this other killing occurred in return for this other killing which we disagreed with.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you've lost me completely. Are you saying that the killings that took place at the medical centre in Kotor Varos were in retaliation for some other killings?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less uncontrolled revenge, an uncontrolled reaction to the killings that had taken place before it was a totally unnecessary, uncalled for reaction.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You're saying -- I'm sorry, it's still not clear. We need to make this clear. The killings at the hospital were an uncontrolled reaction to killings that had taken place before; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, those killings were carried out by whom according to the information that you were given at that meeting and possibly before?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These killings or this uncalled for incident at the health centre was carried out by, I assume, members of the Special Police or some members of the Special Police who were stationed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, that's what you were told, wasn't it, because if we look at the document, at the -- in the second paragraph, Lieutenant-Colonel Peulic is providing you with detailed information about yesterday, that's what the minutes say and say some members of the CSB special unit and other individuals had behaved in and authorised manner. So you were getting on this occasion, no question about it if these minutes are right, Mr. Djekanovic, detailed information from Lieutenant-Colonel Peulic.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I got more information from Dr. Gajanin rather than Colonel Peulic. I think Colonel Peulic wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Wasn't where? Oh, I see, at the killings, sorry, yes. All right, if we go down, we can see that Mr. Tepic informs the Crisis Staff and says that it was his impression that many members of the special unit were acting without authorisation but no one dared to criticise them because of the threats they made. Apart from the killings, what else were the special unit doing?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You already mentioned that part. As far as the matters that I can speak about, as far as the military part of the matter is concerned, the soldiers did have a very, very good professional job and had they not done it like that, the number of victims in Kotor Varos would have been much higher, and in the event that they had not --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Stop, please. I'm asking you what it was that Savo Tepic was complaining to you and the other members of the Crisis Staff was being done by the special unit acting without authorisation.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In extra combat activities, certain members of the Special Police, as well as members of other armed units, other armed personnel, were involved in taking or stealing items from abandoned homes. They would also steal abandoned cars and take them to Banja Luka. And a major part of the aspect of our dissatisfaction, first of all, related to this kind of behaviour by these individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what were they actually doing at the police station to your certain knowledge, Mr. Djekanovic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There were prisoners at the police station, weren't there? Non-Serb --

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were. There was a certain number of persons detained at the police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was happening to those people?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not a question for me. I wasn't at the police station. I know what I had heard, just like you know what you heard, that sometimes there was some improper conduct and beatings, but people who were detained at the police station or those for whom authorised persons recommended measures that they should be -- of detention, they would be in the position to say what happened to them, because in the police station itself there was no space for detention. So there were no detained persons there. I mean, there were some who would spend the night there or something, a certain number of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You talked about the beatings. You knew yourself about the beatings, didn't you? You didn't have to be told by Mr. Tepic.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do you mean I knew about them? That is why there were Crisis Staff meetings where we were all informed about particular areas of activity. I was not at the police station, so I did not know what was happening, and it was not my job to know what was happening at the police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did anybody report to you, not just at the Crisis Staff meetings but elsewhere, that they could hear the beatings?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not receive a report in writing, but we just got information at the Crisis Staff meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was that information that you were getting about the beatings?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got information just like the other members of the Crisis Staff did, that a number of people were detained, that there had been beatings by individuals, and I mean, you can see that I didn't receive anything else in particular about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you yourself hear, as you passed the SJB, any noise?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's too suggestive. No, I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did anybody else tell you that they had heard noises coming from the police station of the sounds of people being beaten?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, I received information at the Crisis Staff meeting. I don't recall anybody else telling me that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'm not going to pursue that. You yourself are recorded as speaking to Mr. Dubocanin about everything going on at the health centre, and that you had been assured by Mr. Dubocanin it would be prevented. Well, what did you say to Mr. Dubocanin about the killings at the health centre?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told him that such conduct in any event is not a good thing. It's impermissible, and it's not good either for the medical centre or for the Serbian people or for the Kotor Varos municipality and that wilful behaviour by individuals should be prevented.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you didn't suggest to him that his unit was guilty of murder?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I did speak with him about the conduct of members of his unit, then the conclusion is that we spoke about the members of his unit. We didn't talk about these things being committed by some others who were outside of their -- or outside of his control.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've just told us that you would report -- it was reported to you that members of the Banja Luka special unit led by Mr. Dubocanin, or he was in charge of them in Kotor Varos, had committed murders outside the health centre. Did you say to him anything about the fact that this was murder?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is being repeated. I already said that this was impermissible, that things should not be done in this way and must not be done in this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. You also apparently said that all these questions had to be cleared up and information provided on the behaviour of the members of the special unit at the meeting with Stojan Zupljanin, the chief of the SCB -- sorry, the CSB, scheduled for tomorrow. Now, you had a meeting, did you, with Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall details, whether on the following day I held or there was held a -- I did have a couple of meetings with Zupljanin. They were not overall official meetings. You can see from the report that we had entrusted the head of the police station, but I don't recall that on the following day a meeting with Stojan Zupljanin was held.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you did, however, have a meeting, didn't you, with Stojan Zupljanin, and you said more than one meeting, but after these killings?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After those killings I did have meetings with Stojan Zupljanin. How many times, when, what the dates were I don't remember, but there weren't many such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. What were you saying to Stojan Zupljanin at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I conveyed to him the positions of the Crisis Staff about our remarks and information, about the conduct of individuals within or as part of the special unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And what did you want him to do?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We wanted him for the unit to be organisationally and structurally constantly under control, that it should not relax and it should not be permitted for individuals to wilfully do the things that we had referred to earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how many meetings -- I'm sorry. And what was his response to that?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case, the event was that he would do everything that was in his power --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- to prevent these people from behaving in the way that they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, who -- who did this -- who was in command of this special unit?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of yesterday's hearing I said that I don't know exactly who it was. According to my information, it was Slobodan Dubocanin. I don't know if it was somebody else, if they changed. I don't know what the structure was and who was at the head of that unit. I said yesterday that I had information that it was Slobodan Dubocanin though.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You say that his response was he would do everything that was in his power to prevent these people behaving in the way that they did. What did you understand he could do?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood that he would prevent that, people wilfully leaving the camp or the base and going to search other people's homes without need to take all of those things and take them to Banja Luka. I particularly asked that we mustn't react uncontrollably in the event that we had certain losses. We had no right to react in such a way towards other people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Searching other peoples homes and things. What about the killings? Didn't you mention those to him?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned later that at the end I did refer to the killings, of course. I did mention the killings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Djekanovic. What did you want him to do about the fact that members of this unit had deliberately and cold-bloodedly killed a number of people outside the health centre?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact is that people were killed, and the fact is that we asked that this should not happen again, that this must not happen again, must not happen again especially in the compound around the medical centre. The fact is that we asked that this stop. Our authority on initiating an investigation or possible criminal reports at the point in time when all of that was functioning in a pretty disjointed manner, when all the institutions were not carrying out their functions, it was not within our jurisdiction to submit criminal reports, but actually now I am aware of the fact that anyone can submit criminal charges or a criminal report if they are able to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I just want to ask you one thing about your answer --

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Submit them to someone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. You say this must not happen again, especially in the compound around the medical centre. Do you mean it was all right if it happened elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you are drawing that conclusion. I am of the opinion that this is something that should not happen anywhere. There was a war. I cannot influence who is going to be killed in the war, but I did believe all other killings, especially after a person had been detained, should not take place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we very quickly just look at one other matter on this set of minutes. It's at page 2 in both B/C/S and English. Under item 3: "Savo raised the question of detainees of whom there are about 73 ..." Was that 73 people in the police station, in the SJB?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this was not in the SJB. This was in detention that was behind the prison building.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "... and what should be done with them. He was told it was a matter for the police to investigate." So it was being left to the police, was it, to decide what to do with these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true that on the basis of a text written the way it is you can draw conclusions that you need to draw, but my view was that those people had to be fed. They had to be guarded. Security had to be provided for that prison. As for what had to be done with them, that was not our decision and there was no decision about whether somebody would be released or sent to a different prison or what you're implying. The activities were to provide food for the prisoner, someone to guard them. All of these things were a source of problems to provide.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may ask that that be admitted as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P81, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we move on, please, very quickly, just to see what happened to the Special Police in Kotor Varos. The next document, please, is, yes, 65 ter 708. This is called -- it's a publication called the "Bulletin" of the Crisis Staff, dated the 26th of June. Was this a document that was issued for the public?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A bulletin was published for a certain period of time in order to inform people in the field, because any other form of communication, because of shortages of electricity, TV, and television, did not exist, and radio. We would issue bulletins from time to time. I don't know how it exactly went from what issue to what issue and from which date to which date.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I just want to deal with two parts of this: In the first paragraph you talk about 15 days of war, 35 men being wounded, all noncritical. "These figures show and remind us that we are in a war that was started to bring about the extermination of the Serbian people from these parts ... we are in a war with an enemy that took the oath of 'Besa' in a holy war, a jihad." We looked at the order of the 19th of December which said you should have propaganda activities. Would this sort of paragraph be classed as propaganda in your view?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If one speaks about the number of losses and that some people went missing, then that cannot be classified as propaganda. It was a fact that there were warring parties opening fire at each other. Everyone knew that. That cannot be propaganda. As for the conclusion, well, that depends on the person. You can draw a conclusion yourself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm asking you. I'm asking you, sir. You're person who arranged for the issue of this document. Do you consider this to be propaganda? Simply yes or no.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the first paragraph as a way of informing. Hence, the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And in the second paragraph: "The enemy is leaderless and in disarray, experiencing heavy losses. Their twin strongholds of Hrvacani and Bilice have been destroyed. We currently control most of the municipality's territory except for the area to the left of the river Vrbanja from Vecici to Ravne." Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what we controlled on this date of the 26th of June. In any case, I think Bilice was completely taken over much later, and I don't know exactly which of these locations fell under our control at what point in time. We did control a lot of the field but even under such circumstances and in those areas and along those roads there were killings daily.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Your Honours, that's all I ask about that document. May that please be exhibited?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P82, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Next can we move, please, to -- it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We alert counsel that we will be taking the break at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I can deal with this last document then. It's -- it's P -- oh, it's already been exhibited. Thank you. P46.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Under item 2: "All those willing to move out of Kotor Varos are to make a statement at the lower court leaving their immovable property to the social political community." And a bit further down. "Ljuboje Gavric is to take part in the Crisis Staff and take responsibility for organising population resettlement." People -- non-Serbs were being moved out, weren't they, of Kotor Varos in a fairly large-scale fashion? That's right, isn't it, Mr. Djekanovic? That's why --

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were people being moved out of the territory of Kotor Varos municipality in different periods of time, in different stages, and for different reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But by the end of 1992, there were hardly any Muslims or Croats left, were there?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was a larger group of Croats from Kotor Varos who moved out even after the signing of the Dayton Accords in 1995. Some large Muslim villages in the area of the municipality remained almost completely populated throughout 1992. People were moving out. There were villages which became completely empty, but it is also correct that there were villages that remained practically intact. To repeat, there were many Croats who left after the Dayton Accords. I don't know on whose orders or whose invitation but it came about after the signing of the accords. We have proof of that. We have arguments.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, which villages remained -- leaving aside Vecici, which was a special case, which villages in Kotor Varos and I'll have the map up, remained populated heavily by Muslims or Croats after 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Siprage, the entire local commune there for the most part. Many Muslims in Garici, Dzube, Maslovare, some in Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown a map so we can follow --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. It's up on -- oh, sorry. It's P65.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: P65? Okay. Perhaps we can blow it up slightly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, which ones do you say, Siprage?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This part here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Maybe the witness can be given the pencil. He can ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know. Yes, fine. Give him one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Muslims remained in this part here. There were some Muslims remaining here. There were many Muslims who remained in the town. Croats remained in Sibovi and Zabrdje up until the Dayton Accords and afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. So apart from those, so we've got --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We've got one village at Garici, one around Siprage, and one around -- I can't read it because you've marked it, but anyhow, near Zabrdje --

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sibovi and Zabrdje, the Croatian population.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As a matter of interest, why when Cirkino Brdo, Hrvacani, Hanifici, and those were all the subject of military operations and the people were in fact expelled, why was that one village allowed to continue? Garici.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one was expelling entire villages. Anyone who did not put up military resistance who did not stake up arms or partake in the functioning of units could -- was allowed to stay. Towards the end of 1992 or even before that, we had Muslim members amongst the police. Towards the end of 1992 in the Municipal Assembly we already had Muslim employees. In TO units, even among those in command, we had Muslim officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Name them, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is this a convenient point, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we just see this and then it would be, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you name any Muslim officers in the TO, please, in 1992 who were in a senior -- in a command position?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Alagic I believe his last name was from Vrbanjci. He belonged to the staff of the TO. He remained with it until the end and worked in the rear units. For a while he even commanded them. In the police Sejdo Tatar remained there who was in command, I believe. In addition to him there were two or three other policemen. In the Municipal Assembly, I made it possible for Mesud Imamovic to come back then Zahinovic who returned from the unit in the field. Later on we had a person working in the boiler room and working on the maintenance of the building. I think his name was Rasim. I was the one who hired him that year.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us the officer -- the police officer you named? You say he was in command. What rank?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sejdo Tatar. I am not familiar with police ranks. I know that he was a capable policeman. He was an athlete, Judoka. I think he was -- his name was Sejdo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You said he was in command. So what was he in command of?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, police doesn't have an extensive command structure. I don't know whether he was an assistant commander or something of the sort. In any case, I know that he worked with those people, cooperated with them. They didn't have command personnel per se.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may. I'm sorry, but there is a procedural matter that popped up in relation to disclosure for the next week for the witness that appears on the videolink. So I believe it's a matter of some urgency, and maybe I suggest that we should either now or that we reserve 15 minutes at the end to address this. I can -- I can briefly inform the Trial Chamber if it pleases the Court. Yesterday we received the disclosure of batch 86. The batch 86 of disclosure contains 32 documents of Rule 68 material for Mr. Basara, the witness which is on a videolink on Monday. We have a deadline tomorrow at noon to provide the court officer with hard copy of the documents we intend to use with Mr. Basara. Unfortunately due to this late disclosure we are unable to even review that, and not to -- not to, I don't know, decide. Of course we will be able to review it by tomorrow and then we have to decide which documents are we going to use for the cross-examination of Basara. Now, we want to ask the Court either to prolong this deadline and that somehow we deal with this situation for the future that, there is -- there is a ruling, for example, that the Office of the Prosecutor is required to provide us with the Rule 68 material at least a week before the witness appears in court. I appreciate the problems, the late searches and all that, but still, this is putting us in a very problematic situation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You will appreciate the difficulties that the obligation under Rule 68 is an ongoing obligation, so it will be impossible to set any time limit for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand it's an ongoing obligation, but we have this witness, which is supposed to appear next week. Of course these documents have been in the possession of the Prosecution for some time, obviously. Therefore, if the search has been done on a timely -- in a timely manner, which means at least 15 days before the witness appears in court, we would have been given these documents on time. Now we received it only yesterday. I don't think that's proper despite the Rule 68 article and the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. This is not something which just appeared at the very late stage. This is something which is in the database of the Prosecution for some time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mrs. Korner, can you explain why it was filed so late?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's not in a database that the Prosecution access same Rule 68. The -- as I've said on a number of occasions, we've explained to Your Honours we had to reorganise our witness list. The searches were originally set out in the order in which we intended to call our witnesses. We moved Basara up. The searches arrived towards the end of September. They were done yesterday, and it's turned up not -- I don't think it would make much difference. Not 32, actually, it's 21, but that's splitting hairs, I accept. And for the majority, the oddity is that there are documents implicating Basara in the crimes in Sanski Most. So, therefore, in one sense they're not Rule 68 at all except that we're calling him as a witness, and that's why we decided they should be called Rule 68. But as I say, they're all fairly short documents. There are 21 of them, and we're just doing our job as efficiently as we. It may not sound like it, but the searches from ISU turned up literally hundreds of documents that in some way related to him. I know because I was doing them on Sunday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But there is a difference between documents that relate to a witness and exculpatory documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but we've got to -- what happens, Your Honour, in case you don't know, we ask the ISU to do a search on the name Branko Basara. They then do the search, provide us with all these documents which -- some of which when we look at them will be Rule 68, many of which are in B/C/S and we can't get translated -- we have to get somebody to read. We get everything that mentions the name Branko Basara, literally everything, and the same with all the other witnesses, because that's what the search is supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So with the best will in the world, Your Honours, and I'm sorry it happened in this way and it shouldn't normally but because of the change in the witnesses, the searches for witnesses who are coming very soon are only just turning up, and we are doing our level best to make sure the Defence get them. As I say, in this case it's not Rule 68 in the way that Your Honours might imagine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So you're saying that these documents are not exculpatory?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: They go -- he is being called as a witness by the Prosecution in the same way as this witness is being called. He was in command of the 6th Krajina Brigade which carried out the crimes in Sanski Most. He's being called to deal with those crimes, and he was interviewed in the same way as this witness was as a suspect. So, therefore, what we're turning up -- but because he's our witness and because the Defence may want to undermine his credibility completely by saying, "You are, in fact, a criminal who committed these crimes," we have been giving them all the documents that relate to the crimes he committed. Now, if that's what the Defence want to do they're entitled to that, and that's why we've seen it as Rule 68. So it's not Rule 68 in the same way as with other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, we are a bit at a loss in understanding what exactly you're asking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are asking for two things: First of all, we are asking to deal with this immediate matter because we have a deadline for tomorrow at noon to provide the court officer with the hard copy of all the documents that we intend to -- to use at the cross-examination of the witness which is appearing over the videolink because the e-court doesn't work there. So that is the number-one problem. That is the acute problem. And the second problem is that we need to -- we need to somehow deal with this situation. Now, in all honesty, I am getting more concerned now than I was before I made the submission, because now I see that there might be some documents which are under Rule 66(B) which have not been disclosed to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let's be very practical and settle this issue quickly so that we can continue with the witness. May I ask you, Mr. Zecevic, when do you -- when would you be able to disclose the list of documents that you -- to the -- to the Registry?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, probably by tomorrow evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: At what time?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But we have the afternoon. I would say 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, the problem, as I understand it, is that because it's a videolink, the documents have to be retrieved physically and brought to -- to Belgrade. Is there any chance --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I know. That's why I'm bringing it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Is there any chance you could make it by, say, 4.00?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're sitting in court until almost quarter to 2.00, so I'll do my best. We're trying to do our best, but I'm not -- we cannot promise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Registrar, when do you leave The Hague -- or what does the Registry leave The Hague?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, we're now currently trying to figure out if you can provide the list of documents by 6.00 tomorrow afternoon. Then we're trying to find out if it is possible for the Registry to identify the documents when they -- and bring them with them physically to Belgrade when they leave Saturday morning. So we'll get back to that. Mr. Pantelic, I hope that it is quick.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Just for the record, Your Honour, what would be discriminating, what would be discriminating for this particular witness is obviously a line of defence of our client, so that should be considered as Rule 68. And in addition, the -- I would like to remind the obligation on OTP on the basis of Rule 66(B) that we have right to inspect all documents in their custody which are material for our defence. Just for the record, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just -- I got -- I got a chance from my assistant's back office. They tell me that a number of documents has not been translated and that might be also a problem, because it is -- as far as I understand, the documents are in Serbian, so then we will have to deal with that somehow. I am just putting the Trial Chamber on notice about that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, on that we don't have an obligation to translate Rule 68, but he's right, they are. Most of them, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't suggesting anything of the kind, that it was the obligation of the OTP, I'm just saying as a fact. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let's bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I should have asked for that map that he marked to be in some way exhibited, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P83, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In fact, I want to stay on maps, please, for a moment, Mr. Djekanovic. During this period, between June and, let's say, the end of July 1992, were you actually living in the town of Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask for the same map to be put up that you marked before, which is P66. And can you just indicate, please, again with the aid of a pencil or whatever that thing is in red, where you were living.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So that's just behind the Catholic church; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A little bit above the Catholic church. The last building has several parts, and some 5 to 600 metres from there is the Catholic church.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And was Mr. Tepic also living in that area?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tepic was living in Kotor Varos, but I can't recall exactly where he lived, if you can believe me. It could have been close to my mother-in-law. I think he rented a flat there. I don't know exactly where. I think certainly he would have had to live there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't worry. All right. How far away from where you were living and where you have marked the SJB were you actually living? I mean, how far was where you were living from the SJB?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The road to the station, I think, is about a thousand metres long, a hundred metres more or less, perhaps, but about one kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you were living a kilometre away from the SJB? Surely not. You've told us the municipal building was only 800 metres from the SJB, and that's considerably further. You were in a matter of yards, weren't you, of the SJB? I can't translate yards into metres, but a few metres from the SJB where you were living, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is your conclusion. I've said, and I pointed out the place where I lived. Where I worked was at the municipal building in Kotor Varos, and I marked that locality. I never lived in any area close to the police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But, I'm sorry, I thought you just marked that blue thing behind the Catholic church. Is that where you were living?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I was telling you. That's where I was living. Next to the Catholic church there was a settlement, a residential area, and I lived in the building that was farthest from the Catholic church.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But the SJB, where you marked it on that map, is very close indeed, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not very far because it's not a big town, but I said that the street or the road between where I lived and the station would have been about 800 to 1.000 metres, a kilometre. I can't tell you exactly and precisely, but approximately thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, we'll hear other evidence about this anyhow, but are you sure you didn't yourself personally hear the screams of people being beaten in the SJB?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to then, please, move very, very quickly, I hope, through the remaining meetings. Did I ask for the last meetings to be exhibited? I think it was 29th of -- yes. It was the 29th of June, Your Honours. Can I have that -- that is exhibited, P46. Very quickly can we look at the 2nd of July, 65 ter 713. Oh, yes, and could we exhibit, I'm so sorry, exhibit that map as marked. Oh, it's already exhibited. It's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Not with the new marking. If you want that to be --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: A separate exhibit. All right. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P84, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think I asked for the minutes, the 2nd July, 65 ter 713 to be put up. In item 3, please. Someone set fire to the Catholic church, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, someone did set fire to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Presumably you must have seen it yourself as you were living right next to it.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see it in that sense. Actually, I was informed that it had been set on fire, and I went there together with members of civilian protection, and we tried to put out the flames. Unfortunately, we were not successful. So I did see it burning. The interior was highly flammable. We tried, I and other -- and members of the civilian protection, to put it out, but unfortunately it was impossible. But I didn't see it from where I lived. I actually came from my office to the spot.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just dealing with destruction of religious institutions in Kotor Varos, nearly every single mosque when the whole municipality was destroyed, wasn't it, during 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the same with Catholic churches?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Catholic church in Vrbanjci Donji was intact. Perhaps a mirror -- a window or so was broken, but that would be about it. Then there was the Catholic church in Zabrdje. That, too, was intact throughout.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then again under item 3: "Considering the situation in the SJB and the behaviour of the special unit members, Ljuban Ecim and Stojan Zupljanin are to be called for interview." So even after the meeting on the 26th of June where the murders had taken place, on the 2nd of July Special Police are still there.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Special Police was still there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you have a meeting with Ljuban Ecim -- or an interview, sorry, and Stojan Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at that time with Ljuban, especially not with Ljuban. The conversation with Stojan came later, and we'll probably touch upon that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, okay. Let's deal with it now, because we're rapidly running out of time. Let's have your -- what conversation did you have with Stojan Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already told you we were privately friends, and on that day when we actually had this meeting there was some kind of military operation where our forces were successful, so that a good number of people from the command of the unit actually participated in this celebration. However, the situation changed suddenly, and some people were taken prisoner. Some people were arrested. The driver of the ambulance was wounded. Some people were taken prisoner, and there was panic. Panic set in in the town itself and also in the ranks of the unit. That is when I went with Mr. Peulic to this location which was over 20 kilometres away from Kotor Varos, and Commander Peulic and some other commanders were there, among them Stojan Zupljanin. This is when I went to object to them, to protest, and to ask that the command and control should be at a higher level and so forth, that it should be raised. That was the substance of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just correction to transcript. It's page 74, line 22. Witness did not say that they were privately friends. He said that they were on kind of private occasion, unofficial occasion, when they met. And also, he didn't say that on -- it was line -- it's page 75, line 5, in transcript it says Mr. Peulic, but I think that witness said that it was Mr. Pejic who was police expected. Maybe my colleague can clarify that or simply witness can confirm.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I went to that locality with the police inspector Mr. Pejic, and indeed this was a kind of private event. So I never had an official meeting with this man, but we took advantage of this -- the private meeting that we had, unofficial meeting that we had to relay our concerns regarding the organisation and so on, and the premature release and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, two questions, first of all. What concerns on this occasion did you express privately to Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this wasn't a private conversation. There were other people there present. We talked about the general situation and the problems that arose, the fact that the men were getting a bit disorganised and less disciplined, and also we discussed the problems that had occurred on the previous days, especially the problems relating to abandoned houses and villages, and that was about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So again you didn't mention killings or beatings to him?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I -- mention was made of everything that was happening, and there was no special emphasis made on that. Of course, we did probably mention those things as well, among others.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And secondly, why -- why have a private conversation with him rather than putting in an official complaint or even going to Zupljanin's superiors?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We communicated officially through the chief of the station, Mr. Tepic. From the minutes, the earlier minutes, it was clearly said that the Crisis Staff could not interfere with military or police matters, and we could only express our opinion or dissatisfaction, but we could not actually tell them what to do or how to do it. In other words, in -- on several occasions in the minutes of the meetings it was said that this was mentioned and that Mr. Savo Tepic would advise him of it and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And whilst we're dealing with meetings with -- with officials, did you ever have any meetings with General Talic about the military?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had many meetings with Mr. Talic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In respect of what? What were you complaining about to General Talic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at -- for a while there was the problem with the personnel in Kotor Varos who were not getting logistical support. Then on other occasions and later on on these occasions where we visited, we had occasion to take a gift to these people or maybe take some supplies if we managed to get some boots or uniforms, pieces of clothing for these people, or we would go and talk simply to encourage each other, to boost each other's morale.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Stop. So you are saying you were taking gifts or clothing or whatever and boots to General Talic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not to General Talic but to the units that he was in command of.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Did you ever make any complaints about what troops under his overall command in the Krajina Corps were doing in Kotor Varos? And that's simply yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And what was it you were complaining to General Talic that his troops were doing in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a general disarray, lack of organisation, overlapping of authorities. Frequently it was not clear who was in command of what unit. We had a Light Brigade in Kotor Varos, as there were in other towns, and there were combat operations in Kotor Varos and yet this Light Brigade was for a very long time without a commander and it was not within the system of the Republika Srpska Army. It was without a commander for a very long time, up until the end of June or maybe even through July. Sometimes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, were you complaining about all this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we were complaining, and we asked them to resolve these issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Okay. Can we move, then, please, to the next document --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Could I have the last one exhibited, please. That's 65 ter 713.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P85, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you look, please, at the 4th of July meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That hasn't been given a 65 ter number, Your Honour, a proper one, so it's 10109. And I'm just going to ask that to be marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Very quickly, item 3. No, it's different. It's different. No. It's completely different. All right. Can I just look at the top page. Does it say the 4th of July at 1730? No. It's the 15th of August. I thought that wasn't right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. I don't want to -- I'll come back to that, Your Honour, if I may, later. Can we move, then -- I hope this one -- to the next one, 65 ter 715, please. There's a complete -- sorry, Your Honour. No, didn't want that one. It's my fault. 7th of July, 717, please. No, that will do. That's fine. 717 will do, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, sir, just very quickly. This is a second -- another bulletin that you issued, is it, of the Crisis Staff activities, but this time on the 7th of July.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, but I believe it's issue number 4. That is the fourth, not the second bulletin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I just want --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not going to go through that because of timing. Could I just have that exhibited, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What for, Mrs. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you want me to go through it I'll explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's full of stuff, but it's just the timing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I realise the timing but you are as much as in control of it. We are hesitant to admit documents that we have no idea about what they say or what they're purported to bring, so please specify and --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I will, does this -- if we look under fight -- the heading "Fighting Becoming Fiercer," do we see these words because you quarreled with my words about takeover: "The takeover of power and attempt to introduce order and rule of law into enterprises agencies ... encountered fierce opposition from forces representing the Croat-Muslim coalition ..." Do you confirm that that's what it says, "the takeover of power." Yes? Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Does it also say that "In addition to active and reserve policemen, the following units participate in this broad scope operation to confiscate arms, special units of the Banja Luka CSB, Serbian Territorial Defence, and units of the 122nd Light Infantry Brigade"?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously that's what it says there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was that accurate? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In operations to collect weapons, all units that were in the field were involved in this in their areas of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in the second paragraph under that first heading "Fighting Becoming Fiercer," do we see: "Still the hardest battles are to come. The fiercest extremists and fanatics have got away to be extremely well-fortified and --" it doesn't make much sense in English, but anyhow, "defended villages of Vecici, Sokoline, Ravne, and some others. Although their jihad is destined to be these parts as our dreams of a Muslim municipality in which Serbs would once again be servants and plebeians, this is not the time to relax because as we've already stated the hardest battles are to come." Did you authorise such language to be put into these documents which were being distributed to the public?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The content of the bulletins was never analysed at the Crisis Staff. There was a man who was in charge of drafting, preparing the bulletin, and printing it off using a very primitive printing device, but we did not discuss the contents thereof at the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But once you'd seen the first one that used this kind of inflammatory language, talking about jihad, did you take any steps to say, This is not language that is going to have an effect of peaceful co-existence, for example? Did you say anything like that?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO DJEKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who, if anyone, was ever able to prove that there was no jihad in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, including our own municipality, and I should add that there were armed forces and that -- they used, and using such a strong term was quite appropriate, because everyone was using them, all sides at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Do you renew your application to have that exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P86, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is it that time, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, we asked Ms. Featherstone if she could speak to you about whether we could sit tomorrow to see if we could finish the second witness, and I think it may be possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mrs. Korner, it looks as if, in fact, the entire afternoon tomorrow might be taken up by this. So we would have to sit literally all day, from 9.00 in the morning until 6.00 or maybe 7.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't -- no. This witness, no. I mean, I honestly -- I know it doesn't sound it, but I only have about another four or five meetings to show him, and I understand -- I don't know whether Mr. Zecevic is able to assist, but I understand that he may be having shorter cross-examination. My application was in respect of the following witness, to try and deal with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, but our concern is that if we take for granted the time indications that the Defence counsels have given, then effectively we will be using all morning with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And then probably most of the afternoon session tomorrow afternoon for the next witness, which would bring us in the end to spend all day in court, and I think that there is an issue, at least with the accused, for them to sit the whole day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because I thought that's rather like the extended sittings that you've organised for the next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: If we had been talking about adding perhaps one extra session of 90 minutes, then we could have discussed it, but it looks more realistic to me that this wouldn't do it. We will have to use at least two if not all three session of tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The Presiding Judge says that it appears to be no as an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I thought we were rising, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: There is a procedural matter with which I must deal. Sir, I must remind you, as I did again yesterday when we adjourned, that your evidence is still ongoing, and therefore I repeat the admonition that you cannot speak to the lawyers from either side, nor can you discuss your testimony with anybody -- your testimony -- in your conversation with anybody else you can't discuss your testimony before the Chamber. So we resume at 9.00 tomorrow morning in this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 9th of October, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25
